matched_finding.subcategory: stated minimum sample size not met
matched_finding.description: The Methods section states that all studies 'collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power).' However, five of the seven included studies fall below this stated minimum: BYU-Sp16 (N=90), BYU-Wi17 (N=90), Gordon (N=80), IIT-Sp17 (N=94), and SAU (N=81). The paper simultaneously claims all studies met the requirement and then reports sample sizes that contradict this claim. This is either a factual misstatement or means studies that violated a preregistered protocol requirement were included without justification or sensitivity analysis.
matched_finding.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)

matched_finding.subcategory: Facebook usage not assessed as covariate or inclusion criterion
matched_finding.description: The study measures perceptions of Facebook specifically, yet Facebook usage frequency was not assessed and non-users were not excluded. By 2016–2017, a substantial proportion of college-aged participants had shifted primary social media use to Instagram and Snapchat. Participants who rarely or never use Facebook would provide meaningless or floor-level responses to Facebook perception items, attenuating true effect sizes and introducing measurement error. The authors acknowledge this temporal confound but do not address it as a potential inclusion criterion or covariate.
matched_finding.quote: both Snapchat and Instagram were among a new crop of social media outlets for US and UK participants that challenged Facebook as the preferred social networking site for the age cohort of the participants in this research

ground_truth.original_snippet: We chose to use the restricted maximum likelihood (REML) model because it has been shown to exhibit less bias than the more commonly used DerSimonian and Laird (DL) model with small numbers of studies (Veroniki et al., 2016).
ground_truth.modified_snippet: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data (Veroniki et al., 2016).
ground_truth.description: Changed principled REML selection (less bias with small k) to post-hoc model selection based on 'more interpretable' results — explicit analytic flexibility

matched_finding.description: The paper prominently claims preregistration as a methodological strength. However, only the individual replication studies were preregistered. The meta-analytic protocol—including study inclusion criteria, analytic model selection, choice of heterogeneity estimator, and outcomes to synthesize—was not preregistered. This distinction is important: decisions made after seeing data (e.g., selecting REML over DL based on 'interpretability') constitute researcher degrees of freedom in the meta-analysis itself. A preregistered meta-analytic protocol would have been needed for the replication badge to extend to the synthesis.
matched_finding.quote: This manuscript qualifies for a Preregistration badge; the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study's OSF page

ground_truth.difficulty_rationale: Unknown missing data procedures acknowledged — must expect this transparency in multi-site studies
ground_truth.original_snippet: Contributors did not always post analysis scripts, so procedures to account for missing data are not known for all studies.
ground_truth.description: Deleted acknowledgment that missing data procedures are unknown for some studies — reader assumes uniform data handling when it actually varied

matched_finding.subcategory: missing data handling undocumented and inconsistent
matched_finding.description: The authors acknowledge that 'not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.' Different approaches to missing data (listwise deletion, pairwise deletion, or imputation) can produce different sample sizes, different variance estimates, and systematically different effect sizes. Without knowing how each study handled missing data, the comparability of effect sizes across studies is uncertain, and the source of any observed heterogeneity is uninterpretable.
matched_finding.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.
